episodes.205136: A high amount of atmospheric moisture in the region interacted with a short-wave trough, allowing for widespread heavy precipitation. This was day four of an extended push of monsoon moisture that produced heavy rain, localized flooding, strong outflow winds.

episodes.205149: Higher moisture moved into eastern and central New Mexico behind a backdoor front resulting in a greater coverage of showers and thunderstorms across the middle Rio Grande Valley, central mountain chain, and northeast New Mexico. Repeated round of thunderstorms resulted in flash flooding on the Ruidoso area burn scars, State Highway 117 in central Cibola County south of Grants and downstream of the Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon burn scar on State Highways 58 and 434 just north of Cleveland and Mora, respectively, in Mora County. Highway 434 in Mora County were closed down for a couple of days to allow for extensive repairs.
episodes.205280: Behind a departing cold front several weak boundaries were left behind across the waters of Eastern North Carolina. As the morning went on, isolated shower and thunderstorm activity developed along these boundaries. Given the lack of instability behind the front only a storm or two became strong in nature bringing an isolated waterspout threat to our coastal waters north of Cape Hatteras.
episodes.205302: Showers and thunderstorms brought flash flooding to portions of southern Utah.
episodes.205550: Deep monsoon moisture led to multiple thunderstorms throughout the day.  Some of the storms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding.
episodes.206748: Scattered storms persisted through much of the day in southern Minnesota, though the strongest cells developed during the late afternoon after destabilization of the atmosphere was able to occur. These storms produced a handful of reported cases of severe hail up to golf ball sized as they traveled southeast and dissipated by around 10pm local time.
episodes.206978: Unusually rich tropical moisture continued to stream over eastern Utah and western Colorado, with precipitable water values in excess of an inch. Combination of upper level support in the form of a jet streak and daytime heating on complex terrain provided the lift to start showers and thunderstorms. These storms, as had been the case in the days prior, were capable of producing heavy rain and high rain rates. Over sensitive terrain, such as slot canyons or recent burn scars, this could cause flash flooding and debris flows.
episodes.207038: A cluster of thunderstorms developed across southwestern portions of the Phoenix area, near the Avondale and Goodyear area and then migrated northeastward into the north Phoenix and Scottsdale areas. With MLCAPE values between 500-1000 J/KG and DCAPE values of 1000 J/KG, it was enough to support isolated damaging wind gusts. In addition, with PWATs of around 1.5, the environment was sufficiently conducive to support some heavy rainfall rates as well, in excess of 0.5 per hour.
episodes.207148: An upper-level trough was positioned in northern Kansas with a 700 mb temperature gradient stretching into SW Kansas with a wedge of high moisture. On the afternoon of the 27th, supercells initiated and produced severe hail and winds. Into the evening, it became a more multicellular regime with widespread heavy rainfall. This produced flash flooding in multiple counties.
episodes.207206: Isolated gale-force wind gusts occurred in association with thunderstorms initially forming along convective island cloud lines.  Later in the evening, and outflow boundary from thunderstorms forming along the southwest Florida Keys produced additional gale-force wind gusts.
episodes.207209: Waterspouts developed from a convergence convective cloud line in the western lee of Key West.
episodes.207271: A significant push of monsoonal moisture brought rainfall to much of Wyoming on 8/27/25. Thunderstorms with high rainfall rates near Jeffrey City led to flash flooding for portions of the town. The public reported ponding water in low spots throughout Jeffrey City. Radar estimates showed 1.0 to 1.5 inches of rain falling on the town of Jeffrey City within a 1 hour period, with up to 2 inches falling west of town. Rainfall rates were estimated to be as high as 6 inches per hour.
episodes.207290: Southeasterly flow advected in monsoon moisture, fueling scattered thunderstorms. A few produced severe winds and dust storm conditions.
episodes.207291: Southeasterly flow advected in monsoon moisture, fueling scattered thunderstorms, some of which produced flash flooding and severe winds.
episodes.207702: Monsoonal moisture surged into the region over a three day period, the most intense of which was the 26th. High atmospheric moisture content combined with weak flow in a monsoonal pattern to produce very moist storms moving very slowly. Additionally, as terrain served as the main trigger for convection, storms would train over the same spots for much longer than normal. Precipitable water was at near record levels around 1.2 inches.

events.narrative: A USGS stream gauge at Lees Ferry (PLFA3) measured a 1.2 foot rise on the Paria River.  Water would likely have been higher upstream closer to the heavier rainfall.  Time estimated by radar.
Flash flooding was reported along Wahweap Creek near Big Water.

Repeated rounds of thunderstorms resulted in flash Flooding along NM Highway 518 just north of Cleveland. A trained spotter observed at least 8 places where small creeks along the Rio Mora were exceeding banks and flooding the highway. Flash flooding also resulted in extreme damage to NM Highway 434. The highway was closed for emergency repairs for 2 to 3 days and was reopened a few days later after installing five corrugated metal pipes and restoring the roadway with a temporary dirt surface.
Minor debris and roadway flooding along SR-359 in both directions near Spanish Springs road.

Rain amounts of 0.2-0.3 inches in an hour caused a debris flow that trapped cars near MP 103 of Hwy 21. This surprisingly small amount of water produced a mudslide because of two important reasons. First, the Wapiti burn scar last year burned very intensely in the flood location, leaving lots of ash and debris on the ground. Second, this portion of Hwy 21 is notorious for avalanches because of it's steep, fairly sparse forest. The very steep open slopes that were primed with ash allowed the small amounts of water to run off almost immediately, carrying debris and mud with it.

A small amount of water in a recently burned area with steep slopes allowed standing water to accumulate to 3 feet next to Hwy 21 near MP 80. This occurred around the same time as mudslides and rockslides on the same highway. While radar captured very little precipitation, this area was known to be susceptible to runoff, especially with the recent wild fires.

Forest Service officials report flooding with ash laden water through House Rock Wash along Buffalo Ranch Road (Forest Road 8910).  The road was impassable and blocked access for BAER team members performing work in the area.  The White Sage burn scar was upstream from this location.
Flooding was reported throughout Incline Village, with multiple reports of closed roads. Upwards of 2.22 inches of rain had fallen over the area.

A training thunderstorm persisted near Arrowrock Dam for about 45 minutes with rain rates between 3 and 6 inches per hour. Rocky cliff faces and steep valleys allowed water to accumulate, though soil/brush retention absorbed most of the rain. While Arrowrock Road was still drivable afterwards, there was evidence of significant water erosion, with multiple spots estimated to have at least 6 inches of running water. The road would have been undrivable during the event.
Rainfall totals at the mesonet station SMDC1 Stampede.
SR-447 closed from Church Street in Nixon to the Pershing Washoe County line.

On the east side of the Valley Fire burn scar, heavy rainfall with a peak rain rate of 7 inches per hour caused a slurry of mud, ash, and debris to flow down eastern Highland Valley Rd, depositing nearly a foot of debris on the road with running water estimated at 12 inches high. The road would have been impassable while water was running, and the debris flow ran down the length of the valley. No impacts along Hwy 21.

Heavy rainfall rates on the recent Valley Fire burn scar created a debris flow that ran down the entire length of Highland Valley, half of which flowed into the Boise River and the other half into a canal. The slurry heavily impacted a community along Warm Springs, running water/slurry could have been anywhere from 3 to 8 ft in height, swept a truck into a fence, only being caught by other debris. Lawns were covered in debris and a white picket fence would have been submerged in the flow. This came from a storm with a peak rain rate of 7 inches per hour that remained over Lucky Peak for an extended period of time.

Following the debris flow that impacted the community at the bottom of Highland Valley, the half of the flow that entered the canal followed the canal into another community near Barber. The flow was so high it crested a canal culvert and began flowing down streets of the suburban community. Multiple inches of silt were built up in the neighborhood, with debris at every turn along the way. Triggering a fast response clean up to reopen the neighborhood.
Three feet of water with mud and rocks covered the intersection of Highways 127 and 190.
Rainfall totals at the mesonet station DEXC1 Dexter.
A gauge on the San Rafael River recorded a flood wave around 700 cfs.

Some noticeable damage observed in a mobile park community home located in the area of Bell Road and 3rd Avenue in North Phoenix. Damage included portions of a wall knocked down; numerous roofs of several mobile homes sustaining some damage including the roof of a mobile home partially torn off; trees uprooted; smashed shingles and bent light posts. Wind gusts were estimated at 55-60 mph. Timing estimated from radar. No injuries were reported.

A Maricopa County Flood Control District Gauge along East Fork Cave Creek near 7th Avenue in North Phoenix showed water levels rose above the alarm stage level of 3 feet, with the flow peaking at 4.09 feet. This increase in water levels above alarm stage likely caused the low-water crossing along 7th Avenue immediately downstream of the gauge location to become impassable. No damages or injuries were reported.

Several large trees uprooted along the roads near Fashion Square Mall in Scottsdale, including a couple of trees along Camelback Road between 64th and 68th street. Wind gusts were estimated at 55-60 mph. Timing estimated from radar. No injuries were reported.
The East Fork of the Virgin River recorded a flood wave of 510 cfs. A flash flood of 1290 cfs was recorded on the North Fork of the Virgin River gauge.
